cards.front: A {{c1::producer}} is a living thing that makes its own food: green plants, algae and phytoplankton.
cards.quote: A producer is a living thing that makes its own food: green plants, algae and phytoplankton.
cards.section: Explain: how a plant makes its own food

cards.front: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
cards.back: Carbon dioxide + water + radiant energy → sugar (glucose) + oxygen.
cards.why: Light supplies the energy; carbon dioxide and water supply the matter.
cards.quote: Photosynthesis uses radiant energy, the energy that travels as light, to build sugar and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water.
cards.section: Explain: how a plant makes its own food

cards.front: In photosynthesis, what does light supply, and what do carbon dioxide and water supply?
cards.back: Light supplies the energy. Carbon dioxide and water supply the matter.
cards.quote: Light supplies the energy; carbon dioxide and water supply the matter.
cards.section: Explain: how a plant makes its own food

cards.front: In photosynthesis, what happens to the radiant energy a plant takes in?
cards.back: The plant transfers some of it into chemical energy, stored in the way atoms are joined. Most of the rest leaves as heat.
cards.quote: The plant transfers some radiant energy into chemical energy, energy stored in the way atoms are joined.
cards.section: Explain: how a plant makes its own food

cards.front: In plants and algae, photosynthesis happens inside a {{c1::chloroplast}}, a green organelle found in some cells, mostly in leaves.
cards.quote: In plants and algae, photosynthesis happens inside a chloroplast, a green organelle found in some cells, mostly in leaves.
cards.section: Explain: where it happens and where the sugar goes

cards.front: Each chloroplast holds {{c1::chlorophyll}}, a green pigment that captures radiant energy.
cards.quote: Each chloroplast holds chlorophyll, a green pigment that captures radiant energy.
cards.section: Explain: where it happens and where the sugar goes

cards.front: Carbon dioxide is only a tiny part of air. Why does it still matter so much to a plant?
cards.back: It enters leaves through tiny openings, and it supplies most of a plant's solid material.
cards.quote: Carbon dioxide enters leaves through tiny openings, and it is only a tiny part of air. Even so, it supplies most of a plant's solid material.
cards.section: Explain: where it happens and where the sugar goes

cards.front: Carbon dioxide is about {{c1::0.04}} percent of air.
cards.quote: Carbon dioxide is about 0.04 percent of air.
cards.section: How much of air is carbon dioxide

cards.front: Name the three things a plant can do with the sugar it makes.
cards.back: Use it now, store it (as starch, in roots, seeds and leaves), or rebuild it into wood and leaves.
cards.quote: Chloroplasts make sugar (glucose), and the plant uses it now, stores it, or rebuilds it into wood and leaves, which feeds almost all other life.
cards.section: Explain: where it happens and where the sugar goes

cards.front: Why does the lesson say photosynthesis feeds "almost every" food web, not every one?
cards.back: Some communities, around deep-sea vents and in a few caves, use chemical energy instead of light.
cards.quote: The exceptions are some communities around deep-sea vents and in a few caves.
cards.section: Explain: where it happens and where the sugar goes

cards.front: A gardener says, "Fertilizer is plant food. That is how my tomato plants get their energy." Is the gardener right?
cards.back: No. The plants make their own sugar by photosynthesis, and light supplies the energy. Soil supplies water and minerals, and fertilizer adds minerals, not energy.
cards.quote: Soil supplied water and a few minerals, so it did not need to shrink by thousands of kilograms.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: Two matching bean plants get the same water and soil. One sits in a sunny window and the other in a dark closet for three weeks. Which will most likely gain more solid material, and why?
cards.back: Most likely the window plant. Light gives its chloroplasts the energy to make sugar, which it rebuilds into leaves and stems. The closet plant makes little or no new sugar.
cards.quote: Light supplies the energy; carbon dioxide and water supply the matter.
cards.section: Explain: how a plant makes its own food

cards.front: In the 1600s, van Helmont grew a willow in a pot for five years. What did he supply, and what did he weigh?
cards.back: He supplied only water and covered the pot to keep out dust. He weighed the dried soil and the willow at the start and after five years.
cards.quote: He supplied only water, covered the pot with a holed metal plate to keep out dust and weighed both again after five years.
cards.section: Evidence: the willow rules out soil

cards.front: Van Helmont's willow went from 2.3 kg to 76.7 kg in five years. His dried soil lost about 57 g. About how many kilograms did the willow gain, and what does that say about soil?
cards.back: 76.7 − 2.3 = 74.4 kg gained, while the soil lost only 0.057 kg. The gain is over 1,000 times the loss, so soil is ruled out as the main source of the mass.
cards.quote: The willow gained tens of kilograms, while the dried soil lost only grams.
cards.section: Evidence: the willow rules out soil

cards.front: Van Helmont's willow numbers rule out soil as the main source of mass. What can they not tell you?
cards.back: They cannot separate air from water, because he measured neither one.
cards.quote: They cannot separate air from water, because van Helmont did not measure either one.
cards.section: Evidence: the willow rules out soil

cards.front: In a gas analyzer at 20 °C, a blueberry leaf in the dark shows a carbon dioxide uptake of −1.09. Did photosynthesis run backward?
cards.back: No. The leaf gave off carbon dioxide because its cells still released energy from sugar.
cards.quote: The leaf gave off carbon dioxide in the dark because its cells still released energy from sugar.
cards.section: Evidence: the blueberry curve

cards.front: Blueberry leaf, 20 °C: uptake was 1.21 at 51 light units and 6.96 at 301. It was 9.73 at 1,000 and 9.95 at 1,500. Compare the gain per light unit in the two ranges.
cards.back: Low range: 5.75 ÷ 250 = 0.023 per unit. High range: 0.22 ÷ 500 = 0.00044 per unit. Light helps about 50 times more per unit at low light, so the curve levels off.
cards.quote: Light, carbon dioxide and temperature change the rate of photosynthesis.
cards.section: Evidence: the blueberry curve

cards.front: A rate curve stays level as one condition keeps increasing. What does that show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: It shows some other limit has taken over. It does not name that limit.
cards.quote: A level curve shows that some other limit has taken over, but it does not name that limit.
cards.section: Evidence: the blueberry curve

cards.front: In the Elodea light experiment, what is the control?
cards.back: One sprig in a tube wrapped in foil, so no light reaches it.
cards.quote: Control: one sprig in a tube wrapped in foil, so no light reaches it.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the Elodea test, you move a lamp closer and the bubbles increase. The closer lamp also warms the water. Can you say light caused the change?
cards.back: Not yet. Temperature may be a second changed variable. Measure and hold it steady, or the test cannot separate light from temperature.
cards.quote: Moving a lamp closer can also warm the water. If bubbles increase, can you tell whether light caused the change?
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A student tests how light affects oxygen production in Elodea by moving a lamp. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable, and two constants.
cards.back: Independent: distance from the lamp (10, 20, 30 and 40 cm). Dependent: oxygen bubbles counted per minute. Constants: plant length, amount of water and baking soda, water temperature, same lamp.
cards.why: Same fair-test rule: change one variable, hold the rest steady.
cards.quote: Independent variable: distance from the lamp: 10, 20, 30 and 40 cm. Dependent variable: oxygen bubbles counted per minute.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: On average a tulip poplar seed weighs under 0.1 g, and one Virginia tree held an estimated 10,000 kg of dry wood. Where did the wood come from, and what did the soil add?
cards.back: Mostly from carbon dioxide in the air, rebuilt from leaf sugar. Soil added water and a few minerals, so it did not shrink by thousands of kilograms.
cards.quote: The tulip poplar's wood came mostly from carbon dioxide in the air.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: A plant's photosynthesis rate has leveled off in the chamber under very bright light. A student turns the light brighter still. What should happen, and what might raise the rate instead?
cards.back: Little change, because light is no longer the limit. Something else, such as carbon dioxide or temperature, may be holding the rate back, so changing that is more likely to help.
cards.why: When changing one condition stops helping, something else limits the rate.
cards.quote: When changing one of them stops helping, something else is holding the rate back.
cards.section: Evidence: the blueberry curve

cards.front: A pond is covered so no light reaches it for weeks. Using the food-web rule, what happens to the phytoplankton, and to the animals that eat them?
cards.back: Phytoplankton cannot make sugar, so little new energy enters the food web. The animals that depend on them, directly or through other animals, lose their energy source.
cards.why: Photosynthesis is the base of almost all food webs.
cards.quote: The exceptions are some communities around deep-sea vents and in a few caves.
cards.section: Explain: where it happens and where the sugar goes
